utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I regret that technical teething problems delayed us with our start this morning. I trust that the three accused can hear me in a language which they understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED RADIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, yes, I can hear. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MRKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I can hear as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SLJIVANCANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Everything is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will not ask that question again during the proceedings but if any one of the accused has a problem understanding what is coming across on the earphones you should draw attention to that problem immediately during the trial. Has there been any change in counsel appearing? I'm looking at Mr. Vasic. Is there any relief at hand for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you for inquiring. I hope that today, in the course of today's day, my colleague, Mr. Vladimir Domazet will join me. He is expected to be appointed as co-counsel in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's good new for you, I'm sure, Mr. Vasic. We look forward to that. I can see all counsel, despite the pillars in the room now. One or two matters of procedure the Chamber would mention briefly. You will all be conscious that at a late stage, it has proved possible to use the new E-Court procedure for this trial. The Chamber is well aware that that may produce difficulties for each team of counsel because there has been only a very short time to prepare your documents for that procedure. We understand, though, that the Prosecution may have been able to get all its intended documents imported into the E-Court system. If that is so, it will perhaps greatly facilitate the presentation of the Prosecution case. But it would seem extremely unlikely that the Defence is yet in that position. The Chamber well understands that you have not had adequate time and we would therefore indicate that in the early stages of the trial, if the Defence finds that it needs a document or documents which it has not been able to import into the E-Court system, the Chamber will readily understand that and paper documents may be used instead of the electronic version. I emphasise that is in the early stages so that efforts should be made to get your documents organised and into the new court system as soon as possible. Both -- generally for the first few days, there will be special technical assistance available to all parties with the E-Court system, but in addition, we understand that for a period at least there will be available specifically to the Defence special technical assistance to assist it with adjusting to the new procedure. That -- the need for that assistance will be monitored. It may well be that it will be convenient for that assistance to be maintained, at least until after the normal vacation in December/January, when there will be opportunity for the -- each team of the Defence to get their -- the papers they anticipate needing for their cases organised into the E-Court system. But that will be monitored as we progress. There are two issues about which we would invite very brief submissions of counsel, not now. We will alert you to the issues and either by the end of today or tomorrow, depending on the convenience of the progress of the evidence, we will hear brief submissions. The first is that under Article 5 of the E-Court practice direction, a time is to be fixed by the Chamber by which the -- in the eloquent language of E-Court the daily bucket of documents is to occur. That is when the documents that will be required for a particular day are to be actually made available to the Registry so that they can be prepared. Now, the issue, I would suggest, is whether that should occur 24 hours or 48 hours before the commencement of the day when the documents will be required. This will be a matter that will equally affect Prosecution and Defence because in due course the Defence will be faced with the same issue. Obviously, it would be easier for counsel if it was only 24 hours, but that limits the time available for action. The time for the daily bucket is also connected to the next issue, the second issue upon which we would receive submissions shortly, and that is whether, once the documents are made available to the Court officer in what I've described as the daily bucket, whether they should also then be made available to the other parties. The -- there are two approaches to this issue. One of them is that documents would not be available to the other parties until they are actually called for in court. The difficulty with that is surprise. The I impracticality and inconvenience of that occurring when counsel will always be taken by surprise by some documents that appear. The particular importance of that in this case arises because of indications in the pre-trial briefs of the Defence that there is objection intended to the authenticity of many Prosecution documents. If there really is to be dispute as to the authenticity of documents, that needs to be known before because the Prosecution will need to bring in the original document if the authenticity is being disputed. It won't be normally possible to have the original document or at least the best copy of it that is available in paper form in court if there is no early notification that a particular document is disputed as to its authenticity. Therefore, it would be most convenient for ensuring the smooth and quick and efficient progress of evidence if documents were provided 48 hours before they were required, not only to the court officer but also to the other parties. And this, of course, would apply both during the Prosecution case and during the case of each of the accused. Then 24 hours before the day in question, the other parties could specifically notify which documents, if any, they disputed as to authenticity, which would then allow the party calling the witness and using the document to have the original or the best paper copy available, ready in court when the document is actually to be used. Now, having put that as a possibility, we will allow counsel to reflect on it and then we'll hear very brief submissions about those two issues at a convenient time, either later today or early tomorrow. There will be some documents which will obviously not be convenient to fully comprehend in the E-Court form. The Chamber, in particular, has on mind maps, photo boards, photographs, sketches and the like. We would indicate to parties who intend to rely on any of those that they should also be prepared to provide paper versions of those. I'm sure all of you have tried at some time or other to study a large map on a small electronic screen, and you will understand what the Chamber is saying when it says that it's often impractical in the electronic form. Where a paper copy is being used in any of the situations that we've mentioned, obviously the party relying on the paper copy will need to provide paper copies to all other parties and to the Chamber, so they will need to be prepared in that way as has been the case to date in all trials that did not use the electronic court system. Now, so far as practicable, the Registry court officer will keep in electronic form each exhibit admitted in the course of the proceedings. Where the original of a document or a paper copy of the document is tendered as the exhibit, such as when the authenticity of a document is questioned or there is a large map, the paper copy of that document, that is the original or the best paper copy available, will be the authentic version of the exhibit, and not the electronic form. Now, they are the procedural matters which the Chamber presently anticipates. There will be one or two more as we adjust into the functioning of the new electronic system. Could I also mention for the assistance of parties that the decisions on the late pre-trial motions that were placed before us in the last week should be expected to be available to you today. And looking ahead, tomorrow morning this Court will be used at 8.30 by another court for what is expected to be a short hearing. Nevertheless, out of caution and for the convenience of everybody, we think we should fix a later time for starting than 9.00 a.m. to ensure that the previous hearing is completed and that the tapes can be recharged and everybody ready. So we would not anticipate being able to start tomorrow before 9.30, rather than at 9.00. All that having been said, Mr. Moore, we look to you now to commence the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think, for the record, I should introduce who I appear with today. I think it's expected on each morning. I appear behalf obviously on behalf of the Prosecution. I'm assisted by Mr. Alex Demirdjian and Ms. Sandra D'Angelo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate that we would normally not trouble counsel to announce movements within the announced team of counsel day by day, but if you arrive with a stranger most certainly announce the new member of the counsel team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And may I just deal with one or two preliminary matters which I have had an opportunity of speaking to my learned friends this morning about? It relates to our first witness, Dr. Bosanac. I went on mission last week and came back late on Thursday night. I saw Dr. Bosanac when I was there and had access to certain material. That has been brought by her to The Hague last night. I again saw her for approximately two hours. There is material which is clearly relevant but has not been disclosed as yet. It relates to records of patients who underwent treatment over a period of time. It has been put into computer form and clearly that has now been brought to OTP, and today is being given its ERN number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My learned friends clearly have not seen the documentation. I suspect Dr. Bosanac will refer to lists and numbers. With the agreement of the Defence what has been suggested is that this topic should not be dealt with by her today or tomorrow but, subject obviously to the Court's leave, that she be recalled if it's necessary to deal with those topics. May I just indicate why it's a matter that cannot be dealt with? What occurred apparently, and I think it's accepted by the Defence, is that patients' records were removed from the hospital in November 1991 and they have never been recovered even though they have been requested by the Office of the Prosecutor. I make no criticism or comment on that. This seems to be a compilation of those records which was subsequently created by others and so therefore it did not manifest itself until I inquired, whether in actual fact there was any documentation in relation to it. So can I just place the Court on notice in relation to that matter? It will not affect the hearing in any way for Dr. Bosanac immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I call, please, then, Dr. Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand you have an injury to your ankle. If you need any different support for it or if it's giving you pain and difficulty at any time, please indicate and we will adjourn or try to make some arrangements to help you. Would you please take in your hand, as you sit, the affirmation card and read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Moore will ask some questions of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What is your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Vesna Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I'm the director of the Vukovar general hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it is correct that you are a doctor of medicine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I am a physician and I am a paediatrician. I also have a master of science degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's correct, I think, that you qualified as a doctor of medicine on the 2nd of October in 1972 at Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, would you please outline to the Court your specialty with regard to your medical experience.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I completed my medical studies in Zagreb. These studies go on for five years. Following that, I worked for one year as a doctor completing my internship in Zagreb, and in 1974, I started working as a general practitioner at the children diseases ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And after --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In 1977, I started my residency training in Zagreb, which I completed in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, after 1981, what did you then do?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I started working as a paediatrician, as a specialist, at the children's ward at the medical centre in Vukovar. I also started my master degree studies and completed a master thesis in social paediatrics in 1983 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is it right that you were then appointed -- in or on the 25th of July 1991, you were appointed the director of the Vukovar general hospital? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. It was actually called the medical centre because in addition to the hospital, the medical centre also comprised all local health centres. It had them under its jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you in very brief outline tell us what the director of the Vukovar general hospital did by way of its role and function?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This was a very responsible post, and a very difficult one, because at the time in the vicinity of Vukovar, there were already many shells landing. The war had already started. We had to organise the work of the entire health services in the vicinity of Vukovar as well as at the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, at a short videotape of the Vukovar Hospital which was taken on and around the 20th of November 1991, and when it's concluded I will ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is to be played in the Sanction format.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I just break it into parts? We see the steps as you enter the Vukovar Hospital, is that right? It's the front of the hospital itself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. We just saw the main entrance into the hospital, which was open on the 19th of November, when actually a large number of civilians from the vicinity came to the hospital in order to find shelter there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the photograph we are now looking at, where is that and where does it go to, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Could you please rewind back just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Isn't that going forward rather than back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's going forward now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us where that is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is the entrance leading into the hallway leading to the basement of the main hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And, doctor, do you know where that is, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is a part of the basement area, where the wounded and the patients were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to assist us with regard to the -- the density of the patients? Was this typical or untypical of the hospital as a whole?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I just interrupt, Mr. Moore? Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I apologise to my learned friend but perhaps it would be useful for everyone what I'm about to propose. Since the witness is testifying about certain segments of the videotape, perhaps it would be good if the transcript reflected the time indicated on the tape so that we could later on know exactly to which part of the videotape certain portions of testimony relate to, since we can see the time indicated here on the screen, and this is related to certain portions of the testimony. Otherwise, once we read the transcript later on, without the footage, we won't be able to connect the testimony to the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Moore, I think you'll be able to accommodate that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we've already been doing that and I can assist in respect of that. I'll do it on each and every occasion I stop, read it out so that it goes into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now at 58.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So the question, doctor, I don't know if you answered it or not, was: The density of beds that we see here, was that typical for the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, this was typical, yes, especially throughout the last two weeks, before the final occupation of Vukovar itself and the hospital. We were not able to evacuate the wounded and sick. We were in no position to take them to their houses, since the town was being shelled by planes and mortars on a daily basis. Nor were we able to evacuate them into any of the nearby civilian shelters where we had medical assistance set up and medical care too, because all the routes, evacuation routes, were cut off to the spare shelter at the commerce Komerc building in Borovo Naselje. So that all the wounded who were brought to the hospital had to stay there. Many of them were lying on the floor. And the situation was truly difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal, please, with the freeze frame at 114.8? Which part of the hospital are we now looking at, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: We are looking at a room in the atomic shelter. This room was specially equipped for very serious patients, for women about to give birth, or for wounded children. This was the only shelter that was safe from being pierced by a plane missile or any of the shells that were falling on the hospital on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again I'd like to deal with freeze frame 1.24.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Which part of the hospital is this, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This is an underground corridor leading from the so-called old hospital building to the so-called new hospital building, where seriously wounded people were accommodated and looked after. Those who -- whose wounds needed to be dressed at least two or three times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, freeze frame 1.38.9, this appears to be a bed within the hospital. Are you able to recognise it or not? I don't mean the exact room itself but its location.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This image shows one of the rooms on the second floor of the new building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were you able to accommodate any patients on the upper floors of the hospital in November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: No, of course not. Hundreds of shells and grenades were falling on a daily basis. That would have been very risky.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how many floors has the hospital, if we take the ground as being the ground, you say this is the second. Were there any floors above it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: There was an attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we look at the photograph for a moment and we look at the wall on the right-hand side, are you able to say what has caused the damage on the wall?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Damage was caused by a shell which was fired from the south of the town, a section that was occupied by the JNA, by the Yugoslav army. What we can see, if we look through the window in this image, is the old hospital building which, as you can see, was also badly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just deal, please, with this building? How many actual rooms, in peace time, did you have that could be used for accommodating patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In peace time, we had 72 rooms on each of the floors. There were rooms for the hospital's personnel. We had surgery rooms. We had intensive care units. Both before the war and now, we have three floors for our patients. The ground floor, the first and second floors in the cellar that is underground, we have diagnostics, we have x-ray, we have laboratories. During the war, during the intense attacks on the hospital, those that began on the 15th of August 1991, all the work that the hospital did went on underground, that is diagnostics, treatment and surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I know it's extremely difficult, or I assume it would be difficult to assess, but are you able to give an indication to the Court when it was you were unable to use these rooms for patients? Can you tell us the month or how it progressed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In August we were no longer able to use those rooms. In early August, we prepared the basement and the atomic shelter for use. On the 15th, I remember, because it's a holiday where I come from, we had a drill on how we could get as fast as possible from the upper floors, from the wards on the upper floors and have the patients evacuated to the shelter in case of heavy air attacks. That was also when the first rounds of shelling began and soon the planes were used to -- soon after, we were no longer able to leave the shelter at all. I'm talking about the shelter where our patients were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with one side issue before I continue with this. You've mentioned shelling. You've mentioned planes. Did the hospital take any steps to indicate or to demonstrate that you were a hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: When the early attacks on the hospital began, the first shell landed on the old hospital administration. I phoned the barracks commander in Vukovar and protested in the strongest possible terms that the hospital was being shelled. After that, we obtained two large signs from the Red Cross, two large Red Cross signs on white canvass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And where did you place those Red Cross signs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: One was placed on the roof of the present administration building. It was the pulmonary ward. At the time the infected ward, that roof was slightly lower so our workers could reach it. The other sign that we had was spread out over the meadow between the two hospital buildings so it could clearly be seen from the air. It was a rather huge piece of canvass. It was white with a red cross on it. Soon after, however, we realised that the bombs and shells were falling precisely on that Red Cross sign and there were many people who said that we should never have placed those signs there to begin with, since they could be used as targets by JNA planes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just assist me by looking at this photograph? You have got clearly in the distance as you ever indicated I think the old billing; is that right? And this photograph is from the new building, is that equally correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we then just consider -- you referred to the meadow where the Red Cross sign was placed. Is it within the vision of the photograph? Can we see where it would be placed or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This specific place is a bit further to the left. You can't see it here but further to the left there is a meadow, an area with grass, where this piece of canvass with the Red Cross on it was placed. There are photographs where that can clearly be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And before we move off - perhaps it's the kiss of death to say finally - are you able to work out or estimate how many times your hospital was hit directly by either bombs or artillery shells from August until about the 20th or 18th of November? Can you give the Court a general estimate?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Between the 15th of August and the 18th of November, each and every day, between 80 and 90 different bombs, missiles, plane bombs or shells were landing on the hospital, each and every day, I say, except on the day of the convoy's evacuation conducted by the Medecins Sans Frontieres in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I want to continue now playing the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with the actual number of people who were in the hospital, let us say, the 18th of November as a guide?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, there were about 450 patients and wounded in the hospital. Those were registered as patients of the hospital. However, on that day, and the next day, plenty of wounded and sick people started streaming into the hospital from the nearby shelters, from the centre of town, who had stayed in the cellars of those buildings and other civilian shelters around town. It is difficult for me to give you an exact figure of patients and wounded persons who were actually in the hospital on the 18th November. One thing we do know for certain, because we produced lists, evacuation lists of hospital patients, is that there were about 450 of them. We had to notify the ministry in Zagreb about the numbers of patients who were not able to move, and those who could still be transported on buses. In addition to the wounded and sick, there were about 300 hospital personnel, physicians, nurses, cleaning ladies, drivers, handymen and their families, their children, wives, husbands. My plan or my idea at the time was that about 700 people would need to be evacuated from the hospital. It's a number that I remember because that was the number of meals that we prepared in the last difficult days when we had no running water, no electricity. On the 18th and 19th of November, as I said, huge numbers of people started coming to the hospital. There were over 500 people who arrived on those two days because it was expected that an evacuation would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the number of patients, are you able to assess what percentage would be civilian and what percentage non-civilian? When I say non-civilian, I'm considering perhaps people who had been fighting in the defence of Vukovar or police. Are you able to distinguish -- were you able to distinguish between those two very general categories or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, yes. It's difficult or impossible to be very specific about numbers, since all the information, all the case histories, of all the patients remained in the hospital building. We had prepared everything for the evacuation. However, only some of the patients and wounded were allowed to bring their case histories with them. Most of the medical files stayed behind inside the hospital building. I myself was taken away on the 20th, early in the morning. I was taken to the barracks. I was arrested and placed in detention. The last time I testified here in The Hague, I asked the Court to try and obtain those medical files for the simple reason that there were many patients, many sick people, who were in the hospital on those days. I'm now talking about all the wounded, all of Vukovar's defenders, all of the police officers, the wounded soldiers of the JNA, the wounded civilians, who were evacuated into Croatian territory. I'm talking about the wounded civilians who stayed behind, who stayed in Vukovar or were later evacuated to Yugoslavia. As we speak, there is not a single medical file dated 1991 at the Vukovar Hospital. There are earlier files, there are later files, but 1991 has been as good as wiped out. I have appealed to the Court already to talk to those in charge. Rumour has it that the files were taken to the military medical academy in Belgrade. It would be very important for those files to be given back, if for no other reason it would allow all the patients who were being treated in Vukovar at the time to have access to accurate information on the injuries sustained and their illness. As we speak, most of those can no longer move and are handicapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I just repeat the question? Thank you very much. Are you able in general terms to distinguish between the percentage of what I will call civilians and non-civilians at approximately mid-November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In mid-November, the ratio was about 50/50; 50 per cent civilians and 50 per cent wounded defenders and policemen. I can't say that this is necessarily accurate. Sometimes my impression is that there were more civilians on that day because wounded civilians were being brought into the hospital. On some days, there seemed to be more defenders but I would say, roughly speaking, the ratio was 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the civilians themselves, are you able to help the Court in assessing the ratio of male-female? Or children?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I have considerable information on that, which I have studied on many occasions. This is based on a database that we had, which before the occupation we used to fax this information to our medical headquarters. We analysed the information. It is very difficult to establish accurate figures because we do not have all the files, but if you would like me to, I would perhaps be able to tell you the number of those who were killed, those who went missing, and those who were wounded in Vukovar. The percentage is very high compared to Croatia in its entirety and to our specific area so --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I'm sorry to stop you for a moment. Can I come back to the question, please? It's my fault perhaps for not putting it precisely. Can you indicate to the Court approximately, when one looks at the civilian category, how many would be female or children as opposed to male? Let's just deal with the civilian and the distinction between male, female, children. Can you do that for us?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Roughly speaking, as I say, between 70 and 80 per cent of the civilians were men and about 15 per cent women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: As for children, wounded children, there was a relatively small percentage. It's a very difficult situation each time a child is wounded. We used to keep children safe in underground shelters despite which there were about 50 children who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: That's based on what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we deal, then, with the injuries, the cause of the injuries to the civilians, please? Are you able, again in general terms, assist the Court with what has caused the injuries to the civilians, male, female, children?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I can't say that with any degree of certainty. Most of the injuries were caused by shells and bombs. For example, a ground floor flat in the neighbourhood of Mitnica was destroyed by a shell. It was a single shell which killed two children, injuring 11. Most of those injured and killed died as a result of JNA shelling. Shells and bombs destroyed virtually the entire town. Just over the last few days I've been thinking about something which I want to share with the Tribunal. Vukovar had 45.000 inhabitants before the war. Over those three months, it was entirely destroyed. This compares to the following situation. It's as if someone were to use planes bombs and grenades to raze the Hague itself to the ground. That's relative to the respective sizes of these two towns, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I deal, then, please, with the method, what I will call the method of delivery of those bombs? You have mentioned aeroplanes. How regularly did you see aeroplanes flying over Vukovar and drop its bombs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Initially, in August and September, it would be once to twice a week. In October, it was practically every day, as well as in November. On the day of the evacuation in October, the evacuation that was organised by Medecins Sans Frontieres, there were no shells. It was a calm day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It might be suggested that these bombs coming from aeroplanes were on targeted military or military targets. Are you able to assist the court whether that is correct or not, from your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I don't know what the term "military target" means, because in Vukovar, the military targets during the occupation and during the blockade, could be, for example, the following: The headquarters of the defenders of the city. It was perhaps one kilometre away from the hospital. The police were stationed in the vicinity of the hospital, perhaps some 200 metres from the hospital. However, the hospital was clearly marked by the Red Cross sign. I heard from the people in Mitnica, which is a settlement located in the border area, where there were absolutely no military targets, that planes were dropping bombs on a daily basis, some of which would start a fire upon hitting the ground, a fire that would consume everything around it. So based on what I know about that, I simply cannot accept this theory that it was the military targets that were targeted in Vukovar, unless the Yugoslav People's Army believed that the entire city of Vukovar was a military target and ought to be completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember the date when the planes started bombing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember. It was on the 25th of August when it happened the first time. That was the day after a group of JNA soldiers was taken from the hospital to the barracks, and a bomb was dropped on the city museum from a plane. There were numerous occasions when bombs were dropped from the planes in the courtyard of the hospital or on the hospital building itself, as well as the two hospital buildings, the former administration building, and the current administration building were all destroyed. I remember that on the 4th of October, two air bombs were dropped simultaneously on the building. One exploded on the first floor and destroyed the rooms on the first and second floor, which can be seen on one of the photographs showing the front facade of the new building. The other bomb went through all five storeys from the roof down to the atomic shelter. However, it did not explode but, rather, landed on a bed where a patient lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's right to say, fortunately, it didn't hit the patient but ended between his legs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. It landed at the bottom of the bed, broke down the bed, and the patient was propelled by that impact and landed on the bomb itself. The patient survived. I remember him to this day. After the occupation, this person remained in Vukovar, but he's doing well now. He's alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. The River Danube, as I call it, flows by Vukovar. That's correct, I think, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. It runs next to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: On the other bank of the Danube, are you able to assist the Court if whether there were any military forces, Serb military forces or JNA military forces, located there? And if they were there, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell you for a fact that there were tanks there, the JNA tanks. I assume they were the JNA tanks. And they were dug in on the left bank of the Danube, directly targeting the city of Vukovar and the hospital. I saw this personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You said that you saw it personally. Did you ever personally see your hospital being hit by what I will call tank or artillery fire from that bank?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I saw that. And I saw that very frequently, almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I may return to this topic but I would like to move on to another area, if I may. I think it's right to say that throughout September, October, November, you were in contact with various, what I will call peace missions, about what you described as the attack on Vukovar, is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to refer you now to a series of faxes which we are going to, with the Court's leave, exhibit. To assist the court, because of the problems with -- of course, they weren't problems, but with E-Court and the possibility that certain matters could not be downloaded into the daily bucket, I created hard copies for all parties just in case the miracle of E-Court would continue. So I have got files that are present for Your Honours and my learned friends, and I can certainly call out the number of the exhibits, but I for my part would like to go through the hard copy and I have similar file for Dr. Bosanac to assist her. So it's going to be almost a hybrid presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be convenient, as long as you make it clear to the Court registry officer each time which document it is that you're turning to in the electronic court numbering so that he can identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm informed actually it's going to be on Sanction, not E-Court, but we will be able to give the numbers so it will not create any difficulties for the Registry. We have got records. If there is any difficulties the Registry can notify me or indeed we can go over them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The concern is that the record, electronically, ought to clearly be able to be identified with your questioning. So that we need to be sure that the electronic number document in the Court system is identified as the witness speaks about a document. So we leave that to you to achieve by a miracle of humanity, if not by a miracle of electronics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The first document which I hope to refer to has got what I will call the ter number 996 and it should be 0 -- in English this is, 0117/2493. Now, if it assists all parties, the way I have done it with the hard copy is that they are all tabulated. There is the translation into English and the original itself. And with the hard copies, there should be an index. We have got tab 1, 2, continuing on the left-hand side. It's at divider 3 on the hard copies. So one goes to the file divider 3, then there should be the index where it says faxes sent by Dr. Bosanac. And then the index itself is the tabulated form, numbering 1 through to 39. The page number for hard copy purposes, not ERN number purposes, on the right-hand, top right-hand corner. The description of the document, the 65 ter number, which will assist all parties, and the ERN number, and I've made sure that the Registry have got a copy of this document and the index so there should be no problems. So if I can deal, please, with -- what I will deal with will be the English version but clearly Dr. Bosanac should have a copy of the first, which for Dr. Bosanac would be page 1, top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this ERN number 01172492?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Correct. So page 1, if I just deal with the last four numbers, 2492 is the original document, the copy, and then page 2, which is 2493, relates to the English translation. And this format hopefully will flow the whole way through logically in sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you proposing to tender each of these in turn?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will be -- I'm quite happy to tender them in turn. Perhaps it's the best and neatest way and then there are no mistakes. Some of the documents I will hardly refer to in any detail at all. Some I will. Perhaps for accuracy, for the Court record, if I do it sequentially and a number can be called out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll proceed, but you realise it will be the electronic form that will be the exhibit with these documents, as I expect none of them are being challenged for authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I say that I personally appreciate having the paper copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think we all do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With we deal, then, please, Dr. Bosanac, with the first document? Can we go to paragraph 3? And it refers, I hope, to on October the 12th, 1991, at 2100 hours, there is reference to a route. Do you happen to have that, doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I just direct you then, please -- because we know therefore that there document is either on the 12th or after the 12th of October, can I direct you then, please, to paragraph 1, where in English it reads as follows, "I responsibly request the principles of neutrality to be respected."? To which agreement are we talking about here when we refer to the route through Zidine being agreed on? How did this arise?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Medecins Sans Frontieres is the only international organisation which responded to my appeals, and tried to organise evacuation of the wounded and sick from the hospital. The first convoy was supposed to arrive at the Vukovar Hospital on the 11th of October. The same route Vinkovci-Nustar-Marinci-Bogdanovci-Luzac-Vukovar Hospital. So this route was supposed to be used. However, that did not take place because the Yugoslav People's Army took the convoy using I don't know which roads to the barracks in Vukovar. The barracks was under the control of the JNA. I heard that they spent the night there, the people in the convoy, and never reached the hospital, but, rather, went back. Then once again in one week they wanted to organise another convoy, which happened one week later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, please, if we look at the document, at the top, we can see that it is directed to the international mission concerning the convoy for the relief aid to the wounded and civilians in Vukovar. It's directed to the Croatian liaison office and signed by you. Now, is it right that this was sent by fax by you or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us where the Croatian liaison office was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we move on, then, please to the next -- what is called tab 2? The original fax is number 0 -- page number 01172494 and it was ter number 996. The English is 01172496. Would you be kind enough, please, to turn up your copy which is clearly, I think -- is that in your handwriting or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not want to interrupt. However, I do have to point out to a technical issue that arose. The previous document and this document can be seen by our clients only in their English version on the screens. However, they were not able to see either of the two documents in the B/C/S version so I wanted to inform the Chamber about that. Perhaps it would be a good idea to give them a hard copy of the B/C/S version so that they could have it before them and could give us instructions regarding that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. It will, I think, be necessary for the Court officer, with these documents that are before him both in English and B/C/S, to try and present both on the screen. If we can move into that pattern now, it will help us later on when we don't have paper versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, contrary to your understanding, I am told that the 65 ter bundle 996 has not been, in fact, received into the electronic system, only the bundle 223. For that reason, it's not possible for the Registry to be displaying the 996 numbers in electronic form in English or B/C/S, unless they can find them quickly on their own resources. So the system cannot work efficiently at the moment. For that reason, I think it will be necessary, with this bundle, and probably more convenient for everybody, to convert to paper because there is this absence from the electronic system of that bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Looking at the time, I think it would be convenient, Mr. Moore, if we had the morning break and if you would please liaise with the Court registry officer to ensure that we can either move efficiently on the electronic court system in dealing with these documents; if that is not possible, to indicate to the Chamber when we return. We have to then make good with paper versions rather than delay. Whichever system is followed, be aware of the concern that there will be need for a B/C/S version to be able to be seen by each of the Accused, whether it be electronic or paper. Could I leave that with you during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Can I -- may I just submit, I had checked to see whether both the exhibits 996 and 223 had gone into the daily bucket and I'm informed that it has. Perhaps another search can clarify. In any event, what I'm having done is hard copies prepared for the defendants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I suggest you liaise so that it can be clear whether there is available on E-Court the bundle 996 or not, and plan accordingly for when we return. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I understand that to overcome some technical difficulties we are now going to proceed on paper. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What we have had done, we have had duplicates prepared for the defendants in paper. They have files of these faxes. So that will be available. We are presenting these faxes in Sanction. 996 and 223 were in the bucket but I think there is really a question of trying to make sure that there is a compatibility. For me it's what I called a VED, a voyage of electronic discovery so we will try and work our way through as best we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hopefully, with experience of a few days we will overcome these technical teething problems and reach the stage where we can enjoy the promised benefits. Yes. Now, you dealt with a document and then moved to another. Are you intending to exhibit the first?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to exhibit all the documents as we proceed sequentially. I seek the Court's guidance in relation to whether it's necessary to distinguish between B/C/S and English. For my part I would have thought not. If they go as a collective exhibit. I'm quite happy for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In paper form you're quite right. When we come to electronic, I think they have to be separately identified, but for paper, at the moment, and we are proceeding on paper, the English and electronic -- and B/C/S form can be received as the one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you tender the first of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I would tender the document that we have mentioned, ending 2492 and 2493, presumably that will be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then move on to tab 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I hope the doctor is able to find it after all that confusion. 2943. No, 2494.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In B/C/S it should be 2494 and 2495 and for the English translation it will be 2496, top right-hand corner for Dr. Bosanac would be page 3, page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: For my part I will be dealing with page 5, 2496. Hopefully the defendants will have now access to all those documents in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, may we deal, please, with the fax that you sent? It reads, "Respected gentlemen." Do you have that particular fax? Are you able to tell us, it doesn't have a date on it, are you able to tell us bearing in mind the last fax was on or around or after the 11th of October, can you tell us when this fax was sent, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: This fax was actually sent on the same day. The substance is the same as the previous fax but it's differently worded. It's in reference to the same evacuation, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to my colleague for interrupting. I have noticed that when the previous document was tendered, we failed to establish the identification number of the exhibit. The Defence was therefore in no position to say anything about it. It's just a matter of principle, really, but I'm afraid at some point sooner or later we will come across a document where that is necessary. At this point in time in relation to this particular exhibit the Defence has no objections to raise but it's all a matter of principle regarding how we tender documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Moore, I am expecting that we will shortly slide into a smooth procedure in which you identify the document by the ERN number and where possible by its date and its tab location as you turn to the document which should overcome the problem of Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I thought I had referred to the ERN number specifically, both in B/C/S and English, so I'm afraid -- I'm sure it's my fault. I don't follow the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Matters not whose fault it is, if you could be sure to do it in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, would you be kind enough, please, to refer to paragraph 1 and then B? If I may read, "If control is necessary, we ask for three members of, 1, the Croatian army, 2, the JNA, and 3, the EC monitors." Why did you ask for EC monitors?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Because we were all very frightened and I felt that I was responsible and that it was my duty to ensure that the evacuation ran smoothly, and that all the wounded and sick persons who were part of the convoy would be escorted safely to another hospital outside Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So when we look at paragraph 3, what did you mean by "that is as a guarantee for a cease-fire"? What was happening at this time that made you ask for a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The situation was getting worse and worse. I'm talking about early October. And shells were falling on a daily basis, as well as bombs being dropped by aeroplanes. These were being dropped on the hospital and its surroundings. I was hoping that if the international organisations stayed in Vukovar together with us it would be easier to reach an end to the aggression against Vukovar and for peace to be restored. That is why I requested that the European Community monitors remain in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we deal, then, finally, with paragraph 5? It reads in English, "In the name of 200 wounded and civilians in Vukovar, please insist that the convoy remains intact." Who was going to be included in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: First and foremost, the wounded, both Croatian soldiers and policemen and civilians. It had been agreed previously that only the wounded could be part of the convoy. The convoy was supposed to come to Vukovar two or three times a week so that it would succeed in evacuating all the wounded and sick. At this point in time there were 200 wounded in the hospital but in addition to those there were plenty remaining in the civilian shelters. Our intention was to have all of them evacuated and brought safely out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Might I make an application for the documents included in tab 2 to be made an exhibit? Presumably that will be Exhibit 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I now move on to tab 3, which has two documents. One is a translation of the other. They are 65 ter number 996. If I deal with the B/C/S ERN number, it's 01172497 and the English translation is 01172497.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to look at page 2497, page 6 in the English format. I will deal with the English version. Here we have got a fax allegedly sent by you dated the 20th of October, approximately one week later on, going to Dr. Christopher Besse of presumably Medecins Sans Frontieres; is that correct? It reads, "I would like to thank you for the assistance you have given us in Vukovar." What assistance had Medecins Sans Frontieres given to you prior to the sending of this fax?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Well, they were the only international organisation that helped us. They came to Vukovar, they helped organise a convoy in which 105 wounded were evacuated. That was the day before the 19th of October. True enough, they brought no assistance in terms of medicines and medical equipment, which is something that we had hoped for. I thanked them nonetheless because they did help to have the wounded evacuated, which allowed them to receive treatment in the free territories of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at the final paragraph, where there is reference to, "We are left now without basic medical drugs and material and without the basic means for treating the injured and the sick." You clearly have indicated this to Dr. Besse. Did you at any time communicate this situation to what I will call JNA sources, to let them know that you were short of medical supplies?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically the first time that I talked to the JNA officers in charge, but by this time I do not think that I had spoken to them directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally, there is a reference to the wounding of nurses in the madness. How did the nurses get wounded?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: One of the lorries carrying the wounded on the way out of town drove over a mine, at least that's what I was told, which exploded. The two Swiss nurses were wounded. It was for this reason that the convoy organiser got in touch with me to tell me that they were sorry but that they were no longer able to continue the evacuation of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I please make application for the tab 3 exhibits, reference 996 and 223, the 65 ter number, 01172497, to be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd like to move to tab 4. Tab 4 relates to a document sent on the same date as the previous exhibit, Exhibit 3. The ERN number is ZA 002325. For the B/C/S. And the English 002326. These are documents which we submit were sent to the Croatian liaison office with the EC mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, would you be kind enough please to look at the top right-hand corner of page 8? The English translation is page 9. It -- I'd like to deal with the first paragraph, please. There is reference to the absolute and immediate withdrawal of JNA from the territory of Vukovar, together with removal of the armaments situated on the left bank of the Danube aimed towards the municipality of Vukovar. Now, when you refer to that, and if you can deal with it fairly shortly, please, the aiming and the armaments are those the same armament or weapons which you have already referred to in your evidence this morning?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Moving to the second paragraph, there is reference to there are still about 170 wounded and 76 -- sorry, 70 sick, including pregnant women and newborn children. Of the wounded, again, are you able to assist the Court with how many of those wounded would be civilian or not civilian?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say with any degree of certainty but I would say 50/50.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is reference then to the medical supplies, on paragraph 3. Paragraph 4, please, "the city of Vukovar is filled with starving women and children and they are determined not to leave their homes." Can you, again in very general terms, indicate to the Court what it was you saw that caused you to add this final paragraph in respect of starving women and children not leaving their homes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Before the siege of Vukovar was complete, that is before the 25th of August, there have been evacuations of women and children to other free unoccupied territories across Croatia. Most of them had returned prior to the 1st of September because it was expected that the school year would begin and that the situation would remain quiet. Several times through the Klajcela [phoen] street hospital in Zagreb and Dr. Fatarini [phoen], UNICEF had tried to have Vukovar's children evacuated. However, their parents would not let the children go and leave. And they themselves had already refused to leave. Some did leave eventually. Some had already left by this time. As I said, there were 45.000 inhabitants in Vukovar before the war. About 15.000 of them remained. These included people who kept refusing to leave their homes. They belonged to all the different ethnic groups, Croats, Serbs, Ruthenes and all the others. So these are the people that I had in mind. When the Medecins Sans Frontieres convoy arrived, a group of elderly people, civilians, who were still uninjured, came along to ask whether they might be allowed to join the convoy too. However, according to a previous agreement, only the wounded were allowed to join. In that group of people who arrived to watch the evacuation, there were no women and children. So this was probably the reason I added this sentence. I know that the town was teeming with women and children still, that they were starving. There was no food to go around. But I didn't go out and look for them specifically to talk to them and try to get them to leave Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I please make application for the documents contained in tab 4, 2325 and 2326, to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I move on, then, please, to tab 5? Tab 5 contains an original document, a fax, and a translation. They are at the following: ZA 002466 in the B/C/S, and ZA 002467, they are subsumed within the 65 ter number of 223.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, would you be kind enough, please, to turn, as I say, to tab 5, your page 10, the English translation is page 11. Here we have a document dated apparently the 21st of October. It's directed to the European monitor mission. Can I deal please with the first paragraph? "I am grateful for your efforts to help Vukovar while under the blockade but I also have to mention that the cease-fire is not respected so that every day there are more and more dead and wounded." And you then proceed to give an example, "on the 28th of October there are eight wounded persons and three unidentified dead persons" and then on October the 21st, "by 11.00 there are 11" -- sorry, "there are eight wounded as well as two dead women." Can I just deal now with the final paragraph? On the day the convoy was in the hospital in Vukovar, a six-month-old dead baby was brought with the head and brain injuries caused by a JNA grenade. The baby was brought by its grandmother, whose right-hand had to be amputated and who barely survived the operation. Are you able to assist the Court how it was that this child and grandmother was injured? What caused it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The grandmother and the child were in the basement of their house. The shell hit the house, making a direct hit on the entrance into the basement, which killed the baby and gravely wounded the grandmother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Later on, you refer to or ask for the or demand for the immediate withdrawal of the army from the municipality of Vukovar, including the village of Marinci. How far away is Marinci -- by way of kilometres, how far away would it be from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Marinci is located about ten kilometres from the Vukovar Hospital, and the road was cut off there at that location, and this was the road that we used before, prior to the full blockade, to evacuate the wounded, the sick, the pregnant women, and so on, and as well as to bring in medical supplies and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us in general terms when that road was cut off and thereby stopped the evacuation of injured and wounded people and the importation of medication?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Most of the roads were cut off as early as the beginning of September. However, there was that road from Luzac-Bogdanovci and onwards which was still operational, albeit with some difficulties because it was constantly targeted by shells and guns, but was still operational up until early October. And from that time on, throughout the rest of October and the entire November, the centre of Vukovar and its environs, were completely or rather fully besieged by the tanks of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm going to spare you the delight of looking at a map at the moment for Vukovar and its general area, but are you able to tell the Court what districts, what roads, were cut off with regard to access to Vukovar and the approximate distance that those districts were away?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Vukovar was completely surrounded, the roads were cut off initially the roads towards Osijek and on. Osijek is 35 kilometres from Vukovar. That road was cut off in the very beginning, and then the next road to be cut off was the road to Vinkovci which is 14 kilometres from Vukovar. At the exit point from Vukovar, the area that is called Borovo Naselje there was another roadblock. In addition to that, in the south, towards the area where the JNA barracks was, there was another roadblock, as well as in Mitnica, leading towards Ilok. Additionally, along the entire left bank of the Danube, there were tanks positioned there, so that was a kind of a blockade as well. In September, it was still possible to go through the corn fields from Luzac towards Bogdanovci, Marinci, to Nustar and Vinkovci. That road was blocked in early October as well. Therefore, 10 kilometres' length of the Danube and the area that was three kilometres wide was the area that constituted the centre of the town, where, in the basements, there were some 15.000 people completely cut off without electricity, water, food, and, on a daily basis, between 9.000 and 12.000 various missiles landed on the city. It seemed that Vukovar was a site where the JNA tested its ammunition, various types of grenades, rocket launchers, aeroplane bombs of various sizes, noxious fumes, toxic fumes, phosphorous bombs, all these things that we had no idea existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. To assist the Court, I will be calling another witness to deal with the -- this topic in more detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make application for the tab 5 documents, ZA 002466 and 2467 to be made Prosecution Exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to point out something that I noticed in this document. However, prior to that, since we are in the initial stages of the trial, could the Chamber please tell us whether, in regard of each document that one side wants to have admitted into evidence, the other side will have an opportunity to raise objections? That's one thing that I wanted to raise. The other thing that I wanted to raise is that B/C/S -- or rather the English version here does not fully correspond to the B/C/S version. I assume that these translations were not done by the CLSS but rather by somebody else and that these translations were used in the book, and if you look at the top of this document, the text does not correspond to the original. In addition to that, if you look at the B/C/S version, it says, eight wounded and three identified dead persons, whereas in the English version, it says eight wounded and three unidentified dead persons. This is something that I noticed just now without any detailed analysis and what worries me is that if these translations were done by somebody else other than CLSS, there could be other mistakes in translation. Therefore, I would like these documents just to be marked for identification so that we can check further the translations and then, should we find any further mistakes, we will notify the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, with respect to your first question, whenever somebody moves for the admission of a document, any counsel who wishes to object to its admission should rise and may do so. With respect to the second, Mr. Moore, can you help me about the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I can say is I clearly operate upon the translation that I have as being accurate and precise. If there are any concerns about the accuracy, if the members of the Defence wish to inform me in advance, or indeed if they subsequently discover there is something that causes them concern, I, for my part, if they wish, can have this matter retranslated or the matter for clarified. I'm quite happy for a procedure to be set in motion which will satisfy both parts or both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Translations have been done by the Tribunal, have they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Some have been done by the Tribunal and some were already in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This has been served on the 65 ter list. I don't criticise my learned friends because of the volume of the documents but clearly one relies on the interpretation itself. I'm quite happy for any concerns that are expressed, for them to be re-checked, as long as the Defence agree with the protocol that will be set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two points of concern were raised. The first is as to the heading of the document which is, I would suggest, not one that's likely to be of significance. It's obvious to the Chamber that there has been no attempt to translate printed headings in the document. The second is whether for the 20th of October there were three identified dead persons or three unidentified. Perhaps you might have that checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I then move on to tab 6? They relate to 65 ter number 223. It's ZA 002323 and 2324 for the English and B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Dr. Bosanac please turn to page 12? And the English version is page 13. I will try and move on as fast as I can. Doctor, I'm going to ask you questions about this particular fax. Please don't feel fettered in any way about giving a full reply, but if you could keep your answers perhaps a little shorter it might help. But do feel free to reply as you deem appropriate. This is a document dated the 22nd of October. There is reference to the EC mission. The first paragraph refers to "we would like to ask you that in your negotiations about Vukovar you present the agreement about a cease-fire because Vukovar is still under artillery fire from mortar shell launchers and tanks on the hospital and on civilian properties." May I deal please firstly, what is the cease-fire that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Very frequently we received information that a cease-fire was being negotiated, and the cease-fire agreement was never honoured, and the only cease-fire that actually did exist was the one that took place during the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just move on to the reference, "since yesterday we have 22 wounded and three dead, mostly civilians," and then you refer to some figures, we remark that in Vukovar since August the 25th, a date that you've already mentioned, until October the 21st, the day before this document was created, in total there was 267 dead, 165 civilians, 4 children, 11 members of the MUP and 87 members of the Croatian army. Now, can I just, please, ascertain how it is you said that there were 165 civilians and four children who were killed? How did you make that assessment of numbers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: What is written here is not an assessment. This is correct data. Definitely correct. We recorded the names of all of the dead and wounded who came to the hospital. This number could be greater only if there were people who were not brought to the hospital. However, these figures here reflect those who were brought to the hospital. We kept our records in accordance with the instructions we received from the Defence staff of the city, and we kept very accurate records of identities of Croatian defenders, civilians, policemen and naturally we knew the identities of the children. In addition to the records we sent on a daily basis to the defence staff of the city, police also kept their records of their members, and the list of the wounded was sent on a daily basis by fax to the medical staff of the medical headquarters in Zagreb. So the figures that are stated here are 100 per cent accurate. They reflect all of those who were brought to the hospital and who were wounded or were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again if you can't assist in relation to this question, please say so. You say 165 civilians, you say four children. Are you able to say the locations of where they received those injuries, geographical locations, whether it's in Vukovar town or in surrounding districts?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: In the city of Vukovar, from Mitnica, Borovo Naselje, and the centre of the town, all the areas that were within the siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How many kilometres is it to Mitnica from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: About five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And Borovo Daci [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: About seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is reference also to three JNA soldiers, Sasa Jovic, and then you go on to name them. What had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: They were wounded somewhere, the positions I don't know exactly where. And the Croatian soldiers brought them to the hospital when they were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And were they treated at the hospital or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: They were treated. A room was allocated in the basement to them and they were lying in beds in that room. They received treatment in accordance with the professional rules. We assigned a doctor to them, Dr. Njavro, who was in charge of their treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why were they given a separate room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The Guards members demanded that or rather the military policemen who brought them there. They wanted them to be kept separate and they wanted them to receive separate treatment, and ensure that nobody would come and disturb them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If it was suggested that JNA soldiers were given inferior treatment at the Vukovar Hospital through this period, would that be a correct assertion to make?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Because that would be untrue. Everybody received everything we were able to provide to them, in terms of medication, bandaging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the previous question was a leading one and my suggestion would be that such questions not be allowed in examination of a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is a fine line on that question, whether or not it is leading. It is proper to direct a witness's attention to a specific issue and I'm inclined to view this question as doing no more than that, leaving to the witness a free hand as to how the witness might respond to what was put. So I thank you for the interjection, Mr. Lukic, but I think Mr. Moore escapes criticism on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Might I make application, then, please, for the documents within tab 6, 2322, 2324, to be made a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is going to be Exhibit number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I then move on, please, to tab 9? Tab 9 is a 65 ter number 223. The document numbers are ZA 002335 and 2336. Tab 9 relates to one document and its translation. That is page 18 for the B/C/S and pages 19 and 20 for the English translation. I hope that's correct. Sorry, I think I have misread the numbers. It should be 2337 and then it should be 2338, 2339. My apologies. But it's certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, could you be kind enough, please, to turn up top right-hand corner page 18 and the English version is page 19 and 20, top right-hand corner.
