Doctor, this is 23rd of October, 11.00 in the morning, "Honourable Sirs," and it's going off to the European mission and the Croatian liaison officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is this a document created by you and sent by you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Here there is reference to, "More than 200 wounded, 76 persons are under the artillery fire from tanks as well as shelled by mortars." And again you repeat about starvation and sickness. Now what I want to deal with, please, on this particular fax, if we move on there is reference, "More than a month we are under the complete traffic blockade. There is neither water nor electricity." Now, did that apply to the hospital or did the hospital have its own power source? Can you just clarify why it was you put in that particular sentence?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The hospital did indeed have a number of its own power sources, but makeshift ones, and we needed fuel in order to run those. And since there was no fuel, we only had enough to use for what was indispensable, surgery, x-ray, lighting in the shelters. However, there was less and less fuel so one of the batteries was struck by a shell and it was often the case that nurses had to treat patients and look after patients by candle light or in complete darkness. Secondly, there was no running water, so we would collect rain water, and we would go to the wells surrounding the hospital. There were six of those. We would go there to get water. We first put chlorine into those wells and then we would get water. Those were old and neglected wells or cisterns but you could still get water there. You had to wait for the water to clear after this initial process. We were not able to go to the river to fetch water because we were within shooting range of the tanks across the river. What this means is that it was very difficult to get anything organised, get anything going, no matter whether surgery, normal health care of patients, or food. For each meal, we needed 600 litres of drinking water. There were 700 patients in the hospital. I could go on about this at great length but I'm not sure if you want me to talk about something very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. That's fine for the moment. Thank you very much. But I would like to just move on to the next part of your first paragraph, because there is reference to "gaseous gangrene." Now, what exactly is gaseous gangrene and how does it -- how is it caused?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Gaseous gangrene is an illness that is caused by an anaerobic infection inside a wound. The gangrene develops in the absence of air. The wound soon begins to fester, tissue is destroyed. The agent enters the blood stream, causes sepsis, and a quick death. This is a very difficult form of death because this is a gram negative infection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is gaseous gangrene, is it capable of treatment with the correct medication?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. It can be treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you have any --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: And we.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- at a time --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: And we did. We had some of it but by no means all. We administered large doses of crystal penicillin. We drained and cleaned the wounds. But this sort of illness calls for further treatment, and in order to do that, you would need to isolate these patients from all other patients who are not suffering from this infection. You need antibiotics, using a biogram, a sample which is taken from the infected area, but we had no equipment to use for purposes of identifying the specific agent. Therefore, we could not select the best possible antibiotic to use against the agent. The most difficult thing for my colleagues and myself, as well as the nurses, was the fact that we knew we were in no position to offer the best possible care, that under different circumstances we could, if this wasn't wartime and if this wasn't the Vukovar Hospital. So that was the hardest thing that we had to face at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Finally this, there is reference in the document about bodies not being properly buried. And you have told us about collecting rain water and also water from wells. Was there any concern that by collecting water in this way, that it would have a significant effect upon the health of the patients receiving that water or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Certainly. In one of those faxes, I'm not sure if in this specific one or not, I asked for the shooting to stop tore an evacuation to take place and for anti-epidemic measures to be taken. That the area be cleansed and that the wells be cleaned. Under the conditions that prevailed at the time, we did our best to keep the situation from further deteriorating, but I believe that despite the conditions, we were to some degree successful. We worked for three months under these impossible circumstances. I should say abnormal circumstances. Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I make an application, please for the tab 9 documents to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's 2337, 2338, and 2339 and I -- might I ask, then, please, the Court to return to tab 7, page 14, top right-hand corner? This is ZA 002333 and 2334 from 65 ter number 223, page 14 for the B/C/S and page 15 for the English version. Can I just say, and I hope I'm correct in this, in actual fact when one looks at the English version, Mr. Lukic I'm sure will assist in this, there is the reference to the defence of Vukovar. In actual fact I think it should say if one looks at the original, it should relate to Vinkovci and not Vukovar. So if the court are minded to accept that and there is no objection, the pen should be put through the word "Vukovar," the defence of Vukovar, and it should be V-i-n-k-o-v-c-i. I think I see everybody is nodding in agreement. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I deal, then, please, Dr. Bosanac, with regard to your page 14, a short document, I think it's right to say what happened -- just a moment, doctor. I think there is a question maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's been pointed out to me that when the last exhibit was received, no number was recorded in the transcript. It was, of course, Exhibit 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. I'm hoping it would be Exhibit 6. 7? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit 7 and we are now back to tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Quite correct. Thank you for that. So tab 9 would be Prosecution Exhibit 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I turn then to page 15, page 14 for Dr. Bosanac? If one looks at the original, this is in your writing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the method of transmission shows that it was forwarded on. Is that right or not? Can you explain how this fax was sent?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The fax was sent from the police building at the Vinkovci Defence staff. That's what the number tells you, 21266. I wanted to reach someone outside Vukovar, anyone, and inform them about the attack on the hospital, when a shell landed on the roof and the roof caught fire. The fire soon spread to the hospital yard, where our workshops used to be. It was a huge number of shells, 40, I think, I wrote at the time, but I had no time to dictate this to a clerk. I just hand wrote it and I was off as quickly as I could, to send the fax and convey the image of this moment to someone outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you actually have a fax machine in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. But that part of the office where the fax was had been destroyed by a bomb. So I did not, in fact, have a fax where I was at the time. I just had a phone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So if I can just -- I hope not lead to you this extent. Is it right that what you were saying is that you have a telephone and telephone line which you used but did not use a fax from the hospital? Is that a correct analysis?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you were going to send faxes, what did you actually have to do, if we just deal with the period as a whole?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I had to get whatever it was that I wanted to send, I had to get in a car and go to the defence staff which was near the municipality building and use their fax. Alternatively, I could go to the police building, depending on how heavy the shelling was on a particular day and how much time I had. Once a fax was sent, I would drive back to the hospital. The police was about 200 metres away and the defence staff was in the centre of town and the distance between the hospital and the defence staff was perhaps about one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Shells were falling all along the road. I risked my life each and every time. The people used to tell me that it was a silly idea, that those faxes were not that important. I would only be getting myself killed and there was no one reading them anyway and no one was likely to offer any assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you ever use the telephone to contact anyone?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you at any time contact someone representing the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what did you tell them in relation to the overall condition of the hospital and, as you have described here, the attack on the hospital? Did you tell them about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I said that the hospital was being targeted on a daily basis by shells, guns, bombs. I asked for this shelling to stop. I wanted peace restored. I asked for peace to be restored so that the wounded could be evacuated --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you tell them --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: -- Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And did you tell the person, whoever you were speaking to at what I will call the JNA end, did you tell them about the medical conditions, the absence of water or electricity, gangrene?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you just in very general terms tell us how often you would speak down the telephone line the sort of things you were saying to them? Try and keep it as short as you possibly can, doctor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I spoke several times to General Raseta, who was the representative of the JNA in Zagreb. I also spoke several times to someone from the General Staff, from the reporting centre in Zagreb. They were trying to hunt down General Brovet's phone number for me and they gave me a number in Sarajevo in their local military district. Somehow I managed to get hold of the right number and I spoke to one of the JNA officers probably in charge of that area. I told them I was from Vukovar, that I was the hospital manager, that I wanted the shelling of the hospital to stop, and the other voice came back saying, "How is that possible? We don't believe you. We don't believe that the JNA is shelling the hospital." I said, well, I can see the tanks from where I am. On the opposite river bank. I can see planes flying over of the I told them to use a helicopter to come to Vukovar. I was hoping that if they came, the attacks would cease. If they came to the hospital. I used this tactic several times but to no avail. I even assumed at the time that they didn't believe me. So I asked one of the wounded soldiers at the hospital, whether they were prepared to talk to Raseta, and then is Sasa came along and phoned Raseta from my office. I listened to their conversations, so I'm sure they knew all of this. It's just that they were not prepared to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: They wanted to destroy us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask then please for the documents on tab 8 to be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Tab 7 it is. Yes, it will be received as Exhibit 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to turn to tab 8? It relates to documents again on the 23rd of October and I can deal with this I hope fairly speedily. They are ZA 002335 and 2336, pages 16 and 17 in the hard copy, page 16 for Dr. Bosanac. This is a document that has been forwarded, our page 15, as it was, and there is reference to the 30 grenade shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, who is Colonel Milan Macek?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I sent my appeal to the Vinkovci Defence Staff or headquarters, and they passed it on to the Croatian army Main Staff in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So can I just ask you, please: Milan Macek, who is he, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Milan Macek was the duty officer, at least that's my assumption, at the Croatian army Main Staff in Zagreb. He received my appeal from Vinkovci and then passed it on to the European Community mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I ask, please, for the tab 8 documents 2232335 and 2236 [sic] to be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I move on, then, to tab 10? Sorry, it's my fault. Tab 9 we have dealt with. Tab 10 it is, yes. It relates to B/C/S and English translations for a letter of the 25th of October, the numbers are 1172507 and they come from the 65 ter document 996. Page 21 is the translation -- I beg your pardon, page 21 is the original, page 22 is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Many of the items that have been included in this letter have already been referred to and I don't wish to repeat it, if it's absolutely necessary. Doctor, if we just look at this letter for a moment, really specifically the first paragraph, "enclosed is a report of the work in the Vukovar Hospital on October the 25th, as you're probably aware on October the 23rd, an artillery attack had started on the hospital and lasted basically for four and a half hours." Now, where exactly did those projectiles land? You refer to a hundred of them.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: They landed on the hospital buildings, in the hospital yard, all over the corridors in which we worked, the cellar. It was a very difficult day. It was one of the most difficult days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I ask, please, for that document to be made an exhibit? That's the tab 10 documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Looking at the time, Mr. Moore, this may be a convenient --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours? Your Honours, my apologies. Before we break, there is something in relation to the exhibit that was given a while ago. I think the translation of the title of this document is inaccurate. The English reads, "The medical centre of Vukovar" and the B/C/S just below, this is the heading of the memorandum, and the letter was sent to the European mission and the Croatian office. Maybe my learned friend from the OTP can ask the witness to have this confirmed thereby dispelling any doubt and this would also save us a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly. Might I do that? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, would you be kind enough, please, to go to page 21, top right-hand corner? I would like you, please, to look at the first typed heading. Would you be kind enough, please, to tell us who it was you were sending that to, or this document to.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The Croatian office with the European mission and the fax number was 041525600, as stated on the face of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think Your Honour was considering this might be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May it please the Court, I'm going to try to move on a little quicker if I can. Perhaps if I could be permitted just to say to Dr. Bosanac that to try and keep her answers short. I hope the Court will allow me that indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I'm going to ask you about the other faxes. We've taken quite a considerable amount of time for the early ones. Could you please try and keep your answers shorter? But if there is anything that you feel needs saying, of course you must do so. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: [No audible response] Thank you very much. Might I then please move to tab 11? That is 65 ter number 223, the ERN numbers are ZA 002342 and 2343. Doctor, would you be kind enough to turning up top right-hand hand side, top right-hand corner, page 23 for the B/C/S version, and page 24 is the English. This document, is dated the 25th of October. It's sent by all accounts to Medecins Sans Frontieres, Mr. Wilna -- I presume it's Mr. Wilna van Artsen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Is this fax, do you repeat, and perhaps extend some of the observations that you have made earlier on?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if needs be, would it be right that you can answer any questions from the Defence in cross-examination on this document, how it was compiled and its contents?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My Lord, might I make application that this document, tab 11, is made a Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And move on to tab 12, please. Tab 12 relates to 65 ter numbers 996 and the ERN number 01172509 and the telephone report is 01172509. And I will be referring to tab 28, in addition to this document, although they will go in upon application as separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we deal, then, please, with page 25 in English, page 26 in B/C/S. There is a reference here from -- a reference to two positions. Why did you name these two positions of Borovo Selo, Lipovaca?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Because in the remaining part of the text, there is mention of the grenades that had been launched from that area. These grenades caused injuries and burns to this patient that is mentioned here, Ivana Ivankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we just deal with this young lady, her name is actually misspelt in this document, but we'll see it later on, her medical records, Silvana Ivankovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was she brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to say whether she was a civilian or a person involved in military activities?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: She was in a uniform of the National Guards Corps and she was brought by the members of the National Guards Corps. Now, as to whether she wore uniform accidently or was a member herself, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And in relation to the extent of the burns, there is reference to second and third degree burns; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: How did you know it was a phosphorus burn?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: When she was brought in, her clothes and her boots were still on fire. We took it off her. It continued burning and it smelled of phosphorus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we turn, please, to tab 28, is it right that therein, on tab 28, if I just give the reference for that, which is page 56 to 50-- or 56 to 61 inclusive, ZA 002449 to 2451, would you be kind enough, please, to turn up page 56 and thereafter? We've got it from 56 to 58 in B/C/S, and I hope the correct translation afterwards; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that young lady survive?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And have you -- are you aware -- I don't want to know the exact address but do you know if she lives in what I will call the Vukovar general area?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. Rather, she lives in the vicinity of Vukovar, in a place near Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in actual fact there is any residual scarring from those phosphorus burns?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I haven't seen her recently, but certainly there must be scars. She underwent treatment following this in Zagreb, in Krapinske Toplica but no doubt the scars remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you, in -- as I will call it, page 25, you are referring to grenades, plural, not singular, was this the only example that you were aware of, of phosphorus grenades being used or were you aware of grenades, plural, being used on various occasions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I know they were used on numerous occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I know because I received calls at the hospital from other parts of the town reporting that bombs were landing, bombs that produced smoke and smelled of phosphorus. I sent the doctors from the emergency room out to go and provide treatment in the areas from which we received reports from of the bombs falling. So I had confirmation from my doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: My Lord, may I make application for tab 12 to be made a Prosecution Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And in relation to tab 28 the medical charts, I equally would make an application for that to be made an exhibit as a separate exhibit. And might I respectfully ask whether it's possible if it could retain the exhibit number of tab 28? Because my intention would be to work sequentially through the documents and the index -- the index is there and it will therefore means that everything stays in sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I look to the court officer to see whether he can accommodate it as Exhibit 28.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So tab number 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you do that I think there may be an objection. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, so far, we attempted to follow the documents presented by the OTP. In this set of documents we received this morning we do not have the tabs but were able to follow so far based on the pagination. However, this last mention of documents, especially the last tab mentioned, we did not quite get and could this be clarified for us so that we can have a clear record of documents admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand the number for the first page is ZA 002449. It bears on it, at the top right-hand corner in my copy, a page 56. And it extends for three pages in B/C/S and then an English translation commencing at page 59. Did that help you at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Page numbers solve all of our problems. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let's hope we can continue to help. Yes, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I then move to tab 13, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, we are holding the last exhibit that you have tendered. We will not receive it at this moment so that it can, in due course, receive the number you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, we have merely 12 exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And one -- the last set of papers being held in abeyance, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the electronic back pocket. May I move on to tab 13, which is from 65 ter number 996, the numbers are 01172518 to 2519. That is, for my learned friend's assistance, pages 27 and 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 27? I'll deal with the first paragraph, we can see it's to the EC mission. There is reference to the protest about positions of the JNA on the left bank, a heavy artillery attack is carried out. Then on the 26th and 27th of October, you refer to 23 heavily wounded two brought in dead and there is reference to nine wounded. It's the last paragraph I want to deal with, please. It reads as follows: "At the moment, in the hospital, in Vukovar, 209 wounded persons are situated among which 70 per cent are civilians and also including the JNA soldiers." Again, as I've asked before, how did you assess who was a civilian and who wasn't a civilian? How did you come to the percentage, approximate, of 70 per cent, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: As I've already explained, we kept records of the wounded to see who was a member of the police force, of the Guards corps, to see who were women and children and so on. Based on that, based on the records, we arrived at the percentage of civilians and soldiers or policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make an application that tab 13 documents to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's numbers 01172518 for the B/C/S, 2519 the English. I will move on to tab 14 in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, can I just ask you to reflect over this period of time? Here we are, we have reached the 31st of October and the first document that we saw, the first fax, was around and about the 12th of October. When one looks at this stretch of time, going to the 18th of November, did matters improve or deteriorate with regard to the conditions in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The matters deteriorated on a daily basis. When the convoy left, the convoy of Medecins Sans Frontieres carrying the wounded, the situation got to be such that every day we had more and more bombs landing, the number of the wounded increased continually, and it became more difficult in every respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And again, looking at that period of time, what about casualties? And I'd like you to focus on what you assessed to be civilian casualties. How did that change?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Every day, on average, 60 to 70 wounded persons would be brought to the hospital. 60 to 70 per cent of them were civilians. My colleagues kept saying that we should not allow civilians to leave the basement at all because they went out to get water, to take some items from their houses and so on, and it was terrible to see how these old people, women, children, were brought back to the hospital half dead, and heavily injured by shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd make application that the tab 14 documents be made an exhibit. That's 1172520, 2521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. May I move on to tab 15, please? Will Your Honour forgive me for one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I move to tab 15, please? Again, the tab 15 documents are English and B/C/S, 996 is the 65 ter number, and it's 01172522, 01172523. To assist my learned friends, the B/C/S is at page 32, the English translation is at page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, doctor, there is reference here, very short entry, about 13.45, 1.45 p.m. as I call it, aircraft have dropped two bombs straight on the hospital, wounded newborn babies, women and patients. Can you remember exactly what happened in relation to this incident? Without going into enormous detail?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that. One of the bombs landed directly on the corridor where there are doors leading to the shelter. This is what prompted me to do this. We were concerned that the entrance into shelter would cave in and, as a result, I wrote this fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I make application for the tab 15 documents, 31st of October, ter number 996 but the ERN number 01172522, 2523, be made an exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we do, could it be clarified what is the nature of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears simply to be a statement. Is it communicated to somebody?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly, I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough please to turn to page 32? Now, it is a typed document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you create this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what way did you create the document and where did you send it to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I wrote this document under unusual circumstances because there was a direct attack on the hospital. So I wrote this down briefly and then forwarded it as usual to the fax of the Croatian liaison office with the European mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That document will be received as Exhibit 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If we then move to tab 16, which is the following day. It is ZA 002463 for the English translation, ZA 002464, the B/C/S, pages 33 and 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 34? Clearly, this is sent to the European mission. I don't want to go through all the details again. It's right to say, I think, that if you were asked any questions about this, you can deal with the questions. You have a recollection; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with one or two parts. If we look at the first paragraph, there is reference to one of the large grenade shells fell on the shelter only to explode in the ground and caved in the entrance of the shelter. Now, what shelter are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Atomic shelter that we were able to see in the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, in the shelter at the time the atomic shelter, there is a reference here, apparently, to newborns, children, pregnant women and mostly severely wounded and injured patients. Can I just clarify, please? Are you saying that these were the people in the shelter at that time or what are you saying or who was in the shelter at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. The people that you just listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you refer to toxic gases, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: What I am referring to are the fumes released when the bomb exploded, which caused people to start crying, and caused shortness of breath and so on. It also reeked of DDT.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The only other matter I wanted to deal with in this document, there is reference on the -- in the fourth paragraph to three ambulances, three ambulances burnt and that you have only one left. How many ambulances did you actually have prior to this incident?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, we had five, and we were given two more by the Caritas. It was part of a donation. All of them were eventually destroyed. We had just one left, and this last one was later destroyed as well. So that the wounded were brought in in vans and civilian cars. There were no ambulances left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can I just inquire, the ambulances that you had, were they marked in any way to distinguish them as ambulances or non-combatants?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: All the ambulances were white with a red cross on them. These vehicles were marked on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'd make application for these or this document to be made an exhibit, ZA 002463, 2464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May we move on to tab 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be given an exhibit number, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could we move, please, to tab 17? That is ZA 002462. This document is a combined document and relates to a telephone message. It's page 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Have you got that, doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This is a telephone message received from Vukovar, from Dr. Bosanac. Now, there is reference here to parachute bombs, most likely Durandal [phoen], bombs used for disabling the runway. Firstly, did you actually see parachute bombs yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I did, when they exploded in the immediate vicinity of the hospital. The bombs exploded when they hit the branches of a tree and then they splintered into myriad small parachutes with small nylon bags attached to them and, once the bags burst, there was some sort of smokey gas coming out. A sort of fog descended on the hospital, which had a strange smell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, there is reference to Durandal, bombs used for disabling runways? Might I respectfully inquire how you know it is that these bombs were used for disabling runways? How did you come about that information?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The people who were in the hospital told me so. They were commenting and that's why I knew, otherwise I would not have been aware of that. This, in fact, was the first time I encountered something like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is reference to multiple rocket launchers. Now, why do you -- and how did you come to the conclusion that there were rocket launchers being used?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I heard this and I saw this. I didn't realise the name was multiple rocket launchers. The reference I heard was VBR, which means the same thing. But they could launch between 60 -- 16 and 30 missiles in a space of 16 seconds. That's something I heard myself but then people told me that they were called multiple rocket launchers because they could fire a series of missiles within a very short space of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to recollect if any of those, as you assess, multiple rockets, did they strike the hospital and the hospital environs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when you say about multiple rocket launchers, are you able to give an indication of how many times you were aware of these being used over a period of time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: They were being used several times every day. It was very difficult to hear them or notice them because the speed of destruction was great, wherever those missiles landed, everything was destroyed. It's difficult for me to say how many times a day. I can give you a rough approximation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Might I apply for the tab 17 document to be made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [In English] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in relation to the questions we heard from the Prosecutor about this document, the witness only provided details about the substance of the document. As for the form of the document, there is nothing to indicate any degree of authenticity. Who sent messages? Who were the messages written to? Perhaps the Prosecutor should ask questions about that so that the witness may be given a chance to clarify who produced this document. Perhaps that would provide additional clarity. All I see for the time being is a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I agree entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor n respect of tab 17, it's a phone call document or refers to a phone call. Do you know firstly whether you made such a phone call, referring to parachute bombs, multiple rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I don't know. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the date here is done as being the 2nd of November. Are you able to say from your recollection whether you made such phone calls in early November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This particular document, do you know where it came from or not? How it was compiled?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: When this was going on, I phoned the Croatian liaison office with the European mission and the health ministry. Judging by the way the document was put together, it is most likely to have been authored by the Croatian liaison office with the European Commission because every time I faxed something or sent them something, they would have a translation done and would then pass it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when one looks at this particular account, does it or does it not correspond with a telephone call that you have made to the Croatian liaison officer or health ministry?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: What I want to try and establish is here is a document which is not created by you but is suggesting that it is a message sent by you. What I want to ask you is if we look at the content of the telephone message, are you able to say whether it corresponds or not with a telephone call that you made?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes. It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you have any remaining concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, I would like this document to be marked for identification so that we could run further checks in order to establish its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The documents at tab 17 will be marked for identification as 17, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. May I move on to tab 18, please? Tab 18 refers to an alleged telephone message from Dr. Bosanac on the 2nd of November, one hour, ten minutes afterwards. It is 01172526 and can be found on the 65 ter number 996. To assist my learned friends, it's page 36 and 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough, please, to turn to page 37? I'll deal with this the way I dealt with the previous one. On November the 2nd, 1991, it's apparently a telephone message received at 12.30 from the hospital in Vukovar and from you. I read it as follows: "After this morning's air attack the hospital is under constant fire. JNA is using multiple rocket launchers from their position around Vukovar. From the territory of the Republic of Serbia, left side of the River Danube, JNA is using long-range machine-guns with explosive bullets also targeting the hospital." Second paragraph: "In the hospital, which is under constant fire are five newborn babies. The last baby was born this morning. Ten infants of age up to six years, 22 school children, and three children unable to move, of age up to 14 years. Also there are seven pregnant women awaiting to give birth any moment. In the name of two and a half thousand children of Vukovar I demand immediate cease-fire from the left side of the river Danube and other JNA positions." Now, let's deal with it the way I dealt with the other. Did you -- having read this document, are you able to say with regard to the content, that you contacted someone in a manner and with the contents that we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Do you know anyone called liaison officer Alan Kosovic? Or did you perhaps is a better way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the date, November the 2nd 1991 --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just wait, I'm sure I'll deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think the nas and the das are getting mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, certainly I heard there was a suggestion of no and then there seems to be a confirmation that it was a yes. So I'm quite happy to ask the questions again if it helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, when you -- I asked the questions again because of a translation difficulty. With regard to the content of this telephone conversation, did you ever send out a telephone call or communicate in telephone form a conversation that deals with these topics?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to the date, November the 2nd, are you able to say whether, when you made that telephone call, whether would correspond with this date approximately, exactly? Are you able to assist us?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When do you think you sent off this message?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I think I sent it exactly on the date stated on this document, 2nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Again I would make application and I suspect my learned friend would equally make application it should be set aside for ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to point out, and what my honourable colleague originally asked the question, is on line 73, line 24, the question was whether she had heard of a person named Alan Kosovic and the witness's answer was a clear "no," whereas the transcript reflects the answer as being "yes." My understanding of the answer was "no." If we could please have this clarified and after that we can speak further about the document. Because the later questions were not in reference to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, perhaps I could speed things up. Noted at the bottom of this document is a name, Alan Kosovic. At that time, in 1991, did you know that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would make application for the tab 18 documents to be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to save time on this. We propose that this document be marked for identification. There is no stamp. There is no signature. And we have not been able to confirm the identity of the person sending the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The person sending it on the evidence is Dr. Bosanac. This is apparently a person who noted the conversation, said to be in the ECMM office in Zagreb. I think as there has been short notice of these documents, they should be -- it should be marked for identification at the moment, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To allow time for further inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. I'm sorry, I heard my learned friend say something. I didn't know whether he was referring to me or not. May we move on to tab 19? At tab 19, relates to page 38, again it's another alleged phone message, 2nd of November, the ERN number is 1172526.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, would you be kind enough to look, please, at the top part of page 38? Again, it's alleged that this was a message given by you. It refers to a grenade attack on the hospital, that they are continuing. One JNA soldier has been heavily wounded near the hospital. His lower extremities had to be amputated. Can I perhaps deal with it this way? Did you at any time contact anyone by telephone informing them that there was a JNA soldier who had been heavily wounded and had his lower extremities amputate? It you please keep your voice up. Can you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when are you able to say when it was that you would make that phone call?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: I phoned, as indicated here, on the 2nd of November. I remember clearly how this happened. If there is time, I can explain. I went to the police headquarters to send a fax. However, the attacks were so heavy that I wasn't able to get there. There was a soldier sitting on the steps outside the police building watching a meal being prepared, was struck by a missile which amputated his leg on the spot. We got him into the car and drove him back to the hospital and the shells were still falling and that's why I remember clearly this event. So, unable as I was to use the fax I had to use the phone to let them know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would make application that tab 19 go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To whom was the telephone call made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, are you able to say to whom it was made, the telephone call was made?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC
utterances.text: The same as before the Croatian liaison office with the European mission. They were the people I called all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the receipt of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same objection, same proposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Marked for identification as 19, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have gone past our time, Mr. Moore. We have been gathering a little pace. Perhaps tomorrow will be more encouraging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must now adjourn, and for the reason indicated earlier today, we will resume at 9.30, if all is well with the proceeding hearing. We adjourn now until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Wednesday, the 26th day of October, 2005, at 9.30 a.m.
